newsitem.title: USA: Crude oil, gasoline prices soar, lumber also rises.
newsitem.headline: Crude oil, gasoline prices soar, lumber also rises.

text.p: Oil prices rose on Tuesday on concerns that a barge accident on the Mississippi River could slow oil shipments headed north.
At the New York Mercantile Exchange, crude oil for April delivery closed $1.14 a barrel higher.
The Coast Guard said the Mississippi River north of Baton Rouge, Louisiana, would remain closed indefinitely as workers clean up after a tow of 25 barges hit a bridge.
The river was already swollen due to flooding on the Ohio and other northern tributaries, traders said. But most expected the situation would improve and not cause shortages of oil products.
"The talk du jour is the Mississippi River. There is a good amount that is shipped, but I think the story is a bit overblown," said analyst Thomas Blakeslee at Cargill Investor Services in New York.

The rally in crude oil jump-started strong gains in refined products, led by gasoline. April unleaded gasoline closed up 2.22 cents a gallon at 67.48 cents while April heating oil rose 1.88 cents a gallon to 56.18 cents.
Traders said the market had been waiting for a seasonal rally in gasoline prices with spring around the corner and ahead of the summer travel season.

"The gasoline market was polishing itself for a rally for quite some time. The Mississippi River story has little to do with it," said John Bradberry, vice president at Transmontaigne Products Services Inc. in Fayettville, Ark.
In weekly data after the close of trading, the American Petroleum Institute indicated gasoline demand is picking up.
Stocks of gasoline in the United States in the week ended March 14 fell 4.32 million barrels to 198.17 million barrels.
Crude oil stocks rose a scant 76,000 barrels and stocks of distillate, which includes diesel and heating oil, fell 3.54 million barrels, the API said.
At the Chicago Mercantile Exchange, lumber futures soared after a strong report on home construction. May lumber closed up $7.90 per thousand board feet at $369.50.

The U.S. Commerce Department said February housing starts rose 12.2 percent from a month earlier to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 1.528 million homes, the strongest home building pace in three years.
However, prices came off their best levels of the day late when cash lumber prices failed to rise in tandem with futures.
"My cash guys were saying there was very little reaction to the housing numbers," said Neil Schmaedick, Smith Barney Forest Products analyst.
Most of the rise in starts appeared to come from increases in building multi-family residences, which use less lumber than single-family units, Schmaedick said.
The strong housing report failed to buoy copper, another key building material.
At the COMEX division of the New York Mercantile Exchange, April copper closed down 1.00 cent a pound at 109.75 cents.
Traders said a fall in stocks of copper in warehouses this week steadied the market but selling pressure had carried over from weakness in other base metals, especially aluminum.
At the Chicago Board of Trade, May wheat futures closed 2-3/4 cents a bushel higher at $3.83-3/4.

Traders cited a forecast from the U.S. Commerce Department on Tuesday predicting the most widespread spring flooding in the United States in a decade, which traders read as a threat to winter wheat about to come out of dormancy.
"That hasn't happened yet, but it might," said analyst Vic Lespinasse of Dean Witter.
